table-page.assembled_note: Exactly the assembly used on the registry, sources, queries and task-run pages: filters, ruler, rows, pagination strip — all in one card.
table-page.placement_note: The filter panel and pagination sit in the TABLE's card, because rows have no frame of their own. Tiles are the opposite: a tile is its own frame, and a shared card would put a frame inside a frame — so the panel and pagination get their own cards, and the grid sits on bare canvas.

part.filters: Filter fields at the top of the card, set off from the rows by a ruler. 12px padding, fields are outlined and comfortable.
part.head: Column labels: 11px, capitalized, muted color — they name the column rather than compete with the rows.
part.rows: A row is clickable as a whole if it has somewhere to lead; hover highlights the whole row, not a single cell.
part.footer: Range, page size and pager in one strip. Its own ruler stays on — it separates the strip from the last row.

breakpoints.note: The "mobile" breakpoint in Vuetify is overridden to md (< 960px): below this threshold the mobile navigation kicks in — overlay drawer and top bar. Reactive state comes from useDisplay() (name, width, mobile).

action-panel.intro: Page actions (refresh button, filter panel, etc.) live in the toolbar on a wide screen, but there's no room on a phone. This prototype lets you mark each action — keep it in the toolbar or move it to the bottom action panel, which only appears on mobile.

kanban.title: Kanban board

edge-scroller.title: EdgeScroller
edge-scroller.note: A reusable wrapper from layout/ for any wide content: horizontal scroll with soft edge shadows that appear on the side where content is still hidden, plus an optional `bleed` prop — pushes content to the screen edges (cancels the page padding) while the first column stays aligned with the heading. The Kanban board uses it; here it wraps a wide table — scroll sideways to see the edge shadows and the bleed to the edges.

part.query: The query string — the only text in the whole field: scopes don't multiply it, they widen the haystack it's searched in.
part.toggles: The toggles go into the append-inner slot, so they sit inside the frame rather than as a separate button group next to it.

part.state: An enabled scope gets an accent fill, a disabled one only the glyph; the same state is announced to the screen reader.

error-states.rule_note: A full-content screen is given when NAVIGATION has died — the person arrived at an address and there's nothing here to look at. If the OPERATION died (a button was clicked, a request failed), the screen must not be taken over: context is worth more, and the answer goes next to the action.
error-states.section_note: Navigation is alive, the shell and menu stay in place. "Not found" is distinguished from a failure by the response status; the backend itself supplies the noun.

offline.form: Message; screen — only if there's no data at all

chunk.case: A chunk failed to load after a deploy
chunk.form: NOT a screen: a silent reload of the same path

page-header.rule_note: The header sits first on a LIST page: the section name there is the page title. A detail page has no header — its frame is the sticky column (see "Detail navigation"): the artifact's name belongs to the artifact and sits in its first card. Both frames share one thing: it's the first thing seen; let a page do without a frame or put it after the content, and arriving at that page reads as a jump. The rule is checked automatically, not kept on trust.
page-header.list_note: Section name, what's in it, actions over the list. No back action: a section is reached from the menu, not from another page.
page-header.detail_note: The same list, but nested inside something — for example a shelf with its research. Hence the back action: arrived here from the parent page, not from the menu.
page-header.loading_note: Until the section name arrives, a placeholder sits in its spot, not emptiness: the page must occupy its space from the first frame, or content would jump underneath it.

part.back: An icon back button, aligned to the TOP edge. Nested sections only. Goes back through history, or to the `back-to` path on a direct visit.
part.title: The page name, the only required part. The `title` slot replaces it along with the tag — for editing the name in place.
part.description: One line about what's on the page.
part.actions: Actions over what's on the page, pinned to the right. Text buttons with an icon — only create gets a filled style.
part.loading: Title and description go into placeholders, back and actions remain: you can leave the page or re-request it even before the data arrives.

sample.list_desc: Research: areas, searches, sources and notes.

detail-nav.rule_note: An object page is built from a sticky column on the left (320px) and content on the right. It has no header: leaving the page and its actions live in the column and stay on screen for the full length of the document, instead of scrolling away with the text. The artifact's name belongs to the artifact and opens the content as a caption above the cards, without a frame around it. The frame is carried not by the view but by the parent route (`DetailShell`): moving from a research item to its area changes only the right half, the column stays put and rebuilds. The rule is checked automatically: a page that fills the column via `useDetailRail` isn't allowed to draw its own frame.
detail-nav.panel_note: The exit takes the full row: the column answers "how to leave from here", not "what to do here", and actions over the object sit next to its name, not here. At the right edge of that same row is an unlabeled gear for appearance. Below the exit is what's used for the whole length of reading: search within the document, a full-width "Copy code" button, and a section outline. All of it comes from the `detailRail` registry, filled by whichever page arrives; the column itself lives in the shared frame and survives transitions.
detail-nav.head: Content header
detail-nav.head_note: The object's name on the left, actions over it to the right of the title, in the same spot on every detail page. The place and look match the actions in `PageHeader` on lists: `variant="text"`, default size, 16px icon, 8px gap. A detail and a list differ in content, not in where to look for "Refresh". Above the name is where the object lives — for a research item that's its shelf, and it's just a link; re-filing happens from the "More" menu.

part.layout: The page grid: a fixed-width column and content filling the rest. Below 1099px it collapses to a single track, the column stops being sticky. Lives in `DetailShell` — one for all detail pages, so only the right track animates on transition.
part.back: There's one way out of a detail page: back where you came from. That's browsing history, and with it the restored reading position. There's no list of higher-up places — the way up is walked the same click at a time, one level per click. The chip's corner is 28px, one line: the exit is recognized by the same shape across the whole app. The label says what the button WILL DO: from history that's "Back", and the place name ("To research list", "To area") appears only on a direct link visit, when leaving has to go specifically there.
part.appearance: The gear in the exit row on a page with a document (`appearance`): clicking it expands a card below the panel with the same fields as the "Document appearance" group in interface settings — typeface, size, line length, code-block font. It's the same setting (localStorage), just at hand next to the text: size and line length get judged by eye against the live body, not against a sample on the settings page. Unlabeled and closed by default — it's about HOW to show the page, not about the page itself.
part.parent: The button's fallback address and label: a direct history-less visit means "back" means "one level up" — with that place's name on the button. Exactly ONE level up: for a source that's its area, not the research item and not the registry.
part.code: The object code is what it's called to the agent, so it's grabbed constantly. Hence two spots: in the header it comes first, left of "refresh" (what belongs to the object first, then what belongs to the page), and in the sticky column — a full-width button right under search, in the row of reading tools. The header scrolls off with the first screen, but the code is needed midway through a long body too. Both buttons carry a label: an icon alone doesn't say WHAT gets copied. The "copied" checkmark is gray — success is told by the icon change, and the code gets copied many times over, so color would read as an event.
part.head: There's no name in the column. The object's name, its place in the tree, and inline renaming — above the content, as a plain caption with no card.
part.refresh: Reload the page. Header buttons carry a label rather than a bare icon: the copy icon alone doesn't say WHAT gets copied, and the button next to the name should read its answer, not have it guessed.
part.more: The last button — "More": rare things done to the object once in its lifetime (re-filing onto shelves). That doesn't deserve its own header button, but an unlabeled ellipsis doesn't need to hide it either. The component holds the button and the list, the page supplies the items — only the page knows their set, and without the slot there's no button at all.

markdown-editor.editorHint: Type "/" for the block menu. An entity code like AREA{'@'}0123456789 becomes a pill as you type or paste it. To the left of a block is the drag handle.
markdown-editor.simpleHint: Only paragraph, bold and italic live here: no slash menu, no drag handles, no block constructs — their nodes aren't in the schema. Paste a heading or a list from the clipboard: the text is kept, the formatting is dropped. The counter below counts the stored markdown and turns red past the limit.
markdown-editor.tableHint: Insert with "/" then "Table". Tab and Shift+Tab move across cells, Tab from the last cell and Enter from the last row start a new one. Columns and alignment are on the panel above the table; the header row can't be removed — without it a table doesn't exist in GFM.
markdown-editor.identicalNo: The text changed — see the differences below
markdown-editor.stableYes: The second pass matched the first
markdown-editor.stableNo: The second pass differs — the serializer is unstable
